quotes.text: They were formed as Brian Poole and the Tremoloes (the spelling "tremoloes" was soon changed because of a spelling mistake in an East London newspaper) influenced by Buddy Holly and the Crickets.

Brian Poole and the Tremeloes first charted in the UK in July 1963 with a pop rock cover version of "Twist and Shout", a song previously popularised in America by the Isley Brothers, and already released by the Beatles in the UK in March 1963 on their first British LP, Please Please Me.

After switching from Decca to CBS Records, with Mike Smith producing, The Tremeloes' first single on CBS was a cover of The Beatles Revolver song "Good Day Sunshine". This also failed to chart, but established a new image of a more contemporary group in tune with the times, which set them up for future continued chart singles as they then started a successful hit run from 1967 onwards.
All members shared vocals, though most of the songs featured either Hawkes or drummer Dave Munden as the lead singer.
Guitarist Rick Westwood sang falsetto co-lead vocal with Hawkes' lower range vocal and group harmonies also featured on "Silence Is Golden".

Their songs were popular with younger music fans and parents rather than rock music fans, although their albums and B-sides included more rock-styled tracks such as band compositions "Try Me" and the instrumental "Instant Whip".
The Tremeloes' pop was as winning and catchy as that of Herman's Hermits, for example, and their songs were a bit more consequential, lacking the teenybopper quality of Noone and his band mates.
To remain relevant as the '60s wore on, countless groups had to reinvent themselves. So it was that by 1967 Brian Poole and the Tremeloes had become simply the Tremeloes.

"Me and My Life" featured a harder, funkier vibe that previous Tremeloes tracks, with a stomping beat that today sounds like the missing link between Summer of Love British popsike, early Bee Gees and – believe it or not – early '70s glam rock a la Slade.
The album is in fact quite good, and far more rocking than one might have expected.
"Wait for Me" rocks really hard, with a gritty lead vocal, a thumping beat, some wonderfully nasty guitar tones throughout, and a searing lead guitar break.
Rarely has a group sounded as much like that era of Bee Gees yet come up with a tune that's arguably better than what the brothers Gibb were turning out. The Leslie-fied guitar work is tasty, too.
Master's failure to find an audience must have had to do with its slightly out-of-time feel; perhaps it's not what fans expected from the Tremeloes.
"Boola Boola" goes through a number of styles, a kind of prog opus writ small.
As an exemplar of the Tremeloes' ambition, the song changes completely into a riffy, psychedelic number that could have sat nicely on the Yellow Submarine soundtrack.
The songwriting team of Alan Blakley (rhythm guitar, keys) and Len "Chip" Hawkes (bass) would be responsible for every single one of Master's tunes.
